results.title: Towards a proposal for assessment of blinding success in clinical trials: up-to-date review: Full Paper PDF & Summary | Bohrium
results.content: Towards a proposal for assessment of blinding success in clinical trials: up-to-date review. # Towards a proposal for assessment of blinding success in clinical trials: up-to-date review. **Research Direction:** Randomized controlled trials ｜ Blinding ｜ Blinding success. Introduction: The Importance of Blinding Success in RCTs. In randomized controlled trials (RCTs), blinding is crucial for internal validity. However, most blinded trials do not report sufficient evidence of blinding success. The article aims to review important issues in blinding, methods for assessment, and propose guidelines. There is a lack of clear reporting on who is blinded, who is tested for blinding success, and how blinding success is assessed. Investigators should clearly describe the blinding methods used. It is recommended to report which key trial persons (participants, healthcare providers, data collectors, outcome assessors, data analysts, and manuscript writers) were blinded. Experiment: Assessing the Success of Blinding. Examples are given to illustrate the assessment and interpretation of blinding data. This includes clearly reporting blinding methods, who was blinded and tested, conducting pretrial evaluations, using appropriate response formats for subjects, reporting data in specific tables, analyzing data with relevant BIs, carefully interpreting blinding impact, and investigating unblinding if it occurs. The CONSORT statement recommended that investigators should clearly report which key trial persons were blinded to treatment allocation and test for the success of blinding. Clinical researchers, however, more often than not overlook the assessment of the success of blinding. The severe under-reporting on the success of blinding may improve with awareness of existing quantitative methods. Assessments of blinding at various points may serve different purposes, i.e. to evaluate comparability between experimental versus control treatments before the trial by the third party; to examine further comparability and credibility of the control treatment and patients' expectation about treatment received in early stage of the trial, and to summarize the overall maintenance of the blinding success at the end of the trial. In this article, we review BIs and how to use these methods along with discussion of other issues in blinding assessment and reporting. Finally we urge the Item 11b of the CONSORT statement to be revised to require the assessment/reporting of blinding success for all trials that adopt blinding schemes.

results.title: Blinding Techniques for Reliable Clinical Trials
results.content: # Blinding Techniques for Reliable Clinical Trials. # Blinding Techniques for Reliable Clinical Trials. Maintaining participant and assessor blinding is crucial for ensuring the validity of trial outcomes. Several clinical trials have successfully employed blinding techniques to minimize bias and ensure the validity of their findings. By understanding the principles and techniques of blinding, researchers can design and conduct high-quality clinical trials that provide reliable and unbiased results. ### What is blinding in clinical trials? Blinding in clinical trials refers to the process of concealing the treatment assignments from participants, investigators, or outcome assessors to minimize bias and ensure the validity of the results. ### How can blinding be maintained in clinical trials? Blinding can be maintained in clinical trials by using techniques such as identical packaging and labeling, sham procedures, and independent outcome assessors. The challenges of blinding in clinical trials include inadequate concealment of treatment assignments, unblinding due to side effects, and insufficient training of investigators and outcome assessors.

results.content: Blinding can be applied to different participants in an experiment, including study subjects, researchers, technicians, data analysts, and outcome assessors. When multiple groups are blinded simultaneously (for example, both participants and researchers), the design is referred to as a double-blind study. Unblinding is common in blinded experiments, particularly in pharmacological trials. Unblinding that occurs before the conclusion of a study is a source of experimental error, as the bias that was eliminated by blinding is re-introduced. In clinical research, a trial that is not blinded is called an open trial. In 1865, Claude Bernard published his *Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine*, which advocated blinding researchers. "Unblinding" occurs in a blinded experiment when information is revealed to someone to whom it has been masked. Some degree of premature unblinding is common in blinded experiments. Thus, the common view of studies as blinded or unblinded exemplifies a false dichotomy. The success of blinding is assessed by asking study participants about information that has been masked from them (e.g., whether the participant received the drug or placebo?). Poorly blinded studies rank above unblinded studies and below well-blinded studies in the hierarchy of evidence. As such, many statistically significant results in randomized controlled trials may be caused by error in blinding. Some researchers have called for the mandatory assessment of blinding efficacy in clinical trials. Studies of blinded pharmacological trials across diverse domains report high rates of unblinding. A 2018 meta-analysis found that assessment of blinding was reported in only 23 out of 408 randomized controlled trials for chronic pain (5.6%). results.title: Blinding during the analysis of research data
results.content: Blinding in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is a strategy that is widely endorsed as a method of reducing the biases that can result from people's awareness of study participants' treatment group status. 50 To maintain blindness, a separate data sheet of the outcome measures will be generated without a record or group I.D. Digital and nurse-led support intervention in primary care during the first year after curative intent treatment for breast or prostate cancer: study protocol of two cluster randomised controlled pilot trials. The absence of blinding, especially when the primary outcomes are subjective, has been found to be associated with inflated estimates of treatment effects, yet little is known about the use of blinding in nursing RCTs. The purposes of this study were (a) to describe the extent to which nurse researchers state that they used blinding as a bias-reduction strategy or explain why it was not used, (b) to identify the groups that are blinded when blinding is used, (c) to assess whether the term blinding or masking is more prevalent, and (d) to explore factors that might affect the use or acknowledgement of blinding in nursing trials. In randomized controlled trials (RCTs), the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle, which involves maintaining study participants in the treatment groups to which they were randomized regardless of postrandomization withdrawal, is the recommended analytic approach for preserving the integrity of randomization, yet little is known about the use of ITT in nursing RCTs. The purpose of this study was to describe the extent to which nurse researchers who conduct RCTs state that they have used ITT, the extent to which they adhere to ITT principles, and the methods they use to handle missing data. Two independent reviewers assessed the feasibility of blinding patients, care providers, and outcome assessors, the perceived risk of unblinding, and whether blinding was reported in 110 reports of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating PT and NPT in patients with hip or knee osteoarthritis. We determined the proportion and 95% confidence intervals of RCTs that reported sequence generation, allocation concealment, randomization implementation, blinding status of participants, health care providers, outcome assessors, and data analysts, sample size justification, method of analysis (e.g. intention-to-treat), and a participant flow diagram.

results.title: Blinding of outcome assessors and its association with outcome in a randomized open-label stroke trial - PMC
results.content: To assess success of blinding, each assessor was asked to guess the patient’s treatment allocation. Assessors may not always be truly blinded for treatment allocation in clinical trials, and their guesses may be associated with outcome. Many trials do not collect information about inadvertent unblinding by patients and proxies or by inadvertent review of other data sources, and, even if collected, trials do not report this information.6–8 We aimed to assess blinding of outcome assessors in a stroke trial with PROBE design and its association with outcome. For this study, patients without guessed treatment allocation (i.e. missing data) by the outcome assessor and patients who died prior to 90-day assessment were excluded. Patients included in the analyses showed similar baseline clinical characteristics, treatment assignment, and 90-day clinical outcomes, as patients were excluded because their treatment allocation was not guessed by the assessor (Table 1). Our study suggests that assessors might not be truly blinded for treatment allocation in trials with PROBE design and that their guessed treatment allocation is associated with outcomes. 12 This assumption might not be true for all trials with PROBE design, as we found that outcome assessors were able to guess the correct treatment allocation more often than expected based on chance. Therefore, it is important that the possibility of unblinding of outcome assessors to treatment allocation is considered and is assessed and reported, as was uniquely done in the IMS III trial. In conclusion, we provide evidence that assessors may not always be truly blinded for treatment allocation in clinical trials, and their guesses may be associated with outcome.
